title: What are the differences between Maven and Gradle?

s1_definition.profdef: Maven and Gradle are both JVM build automation and dependency management tools. Maven is convention-driven and declarative, configured through an XML file called pom.xml, with a fixed, well-known lifecycle. Gradle is a more flexible, programmable build tool configured through a Groovy or Kotlin DSL script, using a directed task graph, incremental builds, and a build cache and daemon for speed. Maven favors standardization and predictability; Gradle favors flexibility and performance.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India has two ways to process a loan application. Maven is like the bank's strict standard form — every branch fills the same boxes in the same order, so anyone can read any application instantly, but you cannot easily add a custom step. Gradle is like giving the loan officer a flexible checklist they can script — they can add custom steps, skip ones that already ran, and process many applications in parallel to go faster, but each officer's checklist can look a little different, so you need discipline to keep them readable.
s1_definition.oneliner: Maven is declarative XML with a fixed lifecycle and strong conventions; Gradle is a programmable DSL with a task graph, incremental builds, and caching for speed.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Maven and Gradle are both JVM build automation and dependency management tools. Maven is convention-driven and declarative, configured through an XML file called pom.xml, with a fixed, well-known lifecycle. Gradle is a more flexible, programmable build tool configured through a Groovy or Kotlin DSL script, using a directed task graph, incremental builds, and a build cache and daemon for speed. Maven favors standardization and predictability; Gradle favors flexibility and performance.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India has two ways to process a loan application. Maven is like the bank's strict standard form — every branch fills the same boxes in the same order, so anyone can read any application instantly, but you cannot easily add a custom step. Gradle is like giving the loan officer a flexible checklist they can script — they can add custom steps, skip ones that already ran, and process many applications in parallel to go faster, but each officer's checklist can look a little different, so you need discipline to keep them readable.

**One line to remember:** Maven is declarative XML with a fixed lifecycle and strong conventions; Gradle is a programmable DSL with a task graph, incremental builds, and caching for speed.

sections.s2_technical:
The first difference is the configuration language. Maven uses XML in pom.xml. XML is verbose but completely declarative and predictable — you describe what you want, not how. Gradle uses a DSL in either Groovy (build.gradle) or Kotlin (build.gradle.kts). Because it is real code, you can write logic, loops, and conditionals directly in the build script. For example declaring a dependency in Maven takes a multi-line `<dependency>` XML block, while in Gradle it is a single concise line `implementation 'org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter-web:3.2.0'`.

The second difference is the build model. Maven has a fixed lifecycle with ordered phases — validate, compile, test, package, verify, install, deploy — and plugins bind their work to these phases. You cannot easily reorder them; the rigidity is the point, because it means every Maven project builds the same way. Gradle uses a directed acyclic graph of tasks. Each task declares what it depends on, and Gradle computes the order. This is far more flexible — you can define arbitrary custom tasks and wire them anywhere in the graph.

The third difference, and often the deciding one, is performance. Gradle has three big speed features. Incremental builds: Gradle tracks the inputs and outputs of each task and skips any task whose inputs have not changed since last time, so it does not recompile unchanged modules. The build cache: Gradle can reuse task outputs across builds and even across machines, so if a teammate already compiled the same code, you download the result instead of rebuilding. The daemon: a long-lived background process keeps the JVM warm and project state in memory, avoiding slow cold starts on every build. Maven historically rebuilds more eagerly and lacks an equivalent built-in cross-build cache, so on large multi-module projects Gradle is typically faster.

The fourth difference is dependency management style. Both resolve transitive dependencies and both can consume the same Maven Central repositories and artifacts. Maven centralizes version management through a parent POM and the dependencyManagement section and BOM imports. Gradle has flexible configurations like implementation, api, compileOnly, and testImplementation, which give finer control over what leaks onto the compile classpath of downstream modules — using implementation instead of api keeps an internal library off consumers' compile classpaths, which speeds up large builds.

The fifth difference is the ecosystem and learning curve. Maven's rigidity makes it extremely easy to read any project — a new engineer opening any pom.xml knows immediately where everything is. Gradle's flexibility is powerful but can produce build scripts that are hard to follow if the team is undisciplined, and the learning curve is steeper. A senior-level nuance: for a bank, the choice is a trade-off between governance and speed. Many banks standardize on Maven precisely because its predictability and uniformity make audits and onboarding easier, while teams with very large codebases or complex custom build logic often prefer Gradle for its performance and flexibility. Both are excellent; the right answer depends on project size and team priorities.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India has a payment-gateway-service and wants to see it built both ways to decide which tool to standardize on across the engineering org.

Problem 1 — a new engineer joins and struggles to understand a teammate's heavily customized build script full of scripting logic. This argues for Maven, whose XML is uniform and instantly readable across every project.

Problem 2 — the monolith takes eight minutes to build on every change, even when only one module changed, and this kills developer productivity. This argues for Gradle, whose incremental builds and build cache skip unchanged work and reuse previous outputs, cutting rebuilds to seconds.

Problem 3 — the auditors want every project to build identically with no surprises. This argues for Maven's fixed lifecycle.

The mini-project shows the same payment-gateway-service configured with a pom.xml and with a build.gradle.kts, declaring the same dependencies and producing the same runnable jar, plus a small Java service class that both builds compile. We show the build commands for each and highlight where they differ.
sections.s4a_structure:
```
payment-gateway-service/
├── pom.xml                 (Maven build definition)
├── build.gradle.kts        (Gradle build definition — same project)
├── settings.gradle.kts     (Gradle project name)
└── src/
    ├── main/java/com/bank/gateway/
    │   └── PaymentService.java
    └── test/java/com/bank/gateway/
        └── PaymentServiceTest.java
```
sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# ---- Maven ----
# Runs the fixed lifecycle: validate -> compile -> test -> package.
mvn clean package
java -jar target/payment-gateway-service-1.0.0.jar

# ---- Gradle ----
# Builds via task graph; reruns ONLY tasks whose inputs changed (incremental).
./gradlew clean build
java -jar build/libs/payment-gateway-service-1.0.0.jar

# Second Gradle build after no changes — notice tasks reported UP-TO-DATE:
./gradlew build          # "BUILD SUCCESSFUL ... N actionable tasks: N up-to-date"

# Run the custom Gradle task (no clean Maven equivalent):
./gradlew printBuildInfo
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input: an engineer changes one line in PaymentService.java and rebuilds, first with Maven, then with Gradle, to compare behavior.

Step 1: With Maven, the engineer runs mvn package. Maven starts the fixed lifecycle at validate, then compile. It recompiles the sources, runs the tests in the test phase, then packages the jar in the package phase. The order is always the same regardless of what changed.

Step 2: Maven does not track fine-grained inputs the way Gradle does, so it compiles the module fresh. On a small project this is fast; on a large multi-module monolith it adds up because unchanged modules may still be reprocessed.

Step 3: With Gradle, the engineer runs gradlew build. Gradle builds a task graph, then checks each task's inputs against the last run. The compile task sees PaymentService.java changed, so it recompiles. But tasks whose inputs did not change are reported UP-TO-DATE and skipped entirely.

Step 4: Gradle's daemon is already warm in the background, so there is no JVM cold-start cost, and if the build cache has a matching output from a teammate, Gradle downloads it instead of rebuilding. The net effect is a much faster rebuild on large projects.

Step 5: Both builds run the same JUnit test, compile the same PaymentService, and produce a runnable jar containing identical application behavior. The gateway-fee logic computes 500.00 on a 100000 payment in both cases.

Step 6: The engineer reruns gradlew build without changing anything; Gradle reports all tasks UP-TO-DATE and finishes in under a second, demonstrating incremental builds, while a second mvn package would re-run the lifecycle again.

```
Oct 25, 2026 12:40:02 AM INFO: [maven] lifecycle validate->compile->test->package
Oct 25, 2026 12:40:19 AM INFO: [maven] BUILD SUCCESS (17s)
Oct 25, 2026 12:41:02 AM INFO: [gradle] :compileJava changed -> recompiled
Oct 25, 2026 12:41:02 AM INFO: [gradle] :processResources UP-TO-DATE (skipped)
Oct 25, 2026 12:41:05 AM INFO: [gradle] BUILD SUCCESSFUL (3s, daemon warm)
Oct 25, 2026 12:41:30 AM INFO: [gradle] re-run: all tasks UP-TO-DATE (0.6s)
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Source change: PaymentService.java edited
    │
    ├─ MAVEN path                          ├─ GRADLE path
    │  pom.xml (XML, declarative)           │  build.gradle.kts (DSL, task graph)
    │  fixed lifecycle:                     │  compute task graph
    │   validate                            │  check inputs vs last run
    │    ↓                                  │   :compileJava  CHANGED -> run
    │   compile  (recompile module)         │   :processResources UP-TO-DATE skip
    │    ↓                                  │   :test  (affected) -> run
    │   test                                │  daemon warm + build cache reuse
    │    ↓                                  │
    │   package                             │
    ▼                                       ▼
  target/...-1.0.0.jar                 build/libs/...-1.0.0.jar
    │                                       │
    └──────────── identical app behavior ───┘
                  gatewayFee(100000) = 500.00
```
sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Build Model Comparison ═══

  ┌─ Key Differences (Maven  <->  Gradle) ───────────────────────┐
  │  Config: XML pom.xml     <->  Groovy/Kotlin DSL              │
  │  Model:  fixed lifecycle <->  directed task graph (DAG)      │
  │  Speed:  rebuild eager   <->  incremental + cache + daemon   │
  │  Deps:   dependencyMgmt  <->  configurations (impl/api/...)   │
  │  Style:  uniform/readable<->  flexible/programmable          │
  │  Both:   consume Maven Central, resolve transitive deps      │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Maven Lifecycle (fixed, ordered) ───────────────────────

  validate → compile → test → package → verify → install → deploy
     (plugins BIND goals to these phases; order is not changeable)

  ── Gradle Task Graph (flexible DAG) ───────────────────────

           ┌────────────┐
           │ compileJava│──┐
           └────────────┘  │ dependsOn
                           ▼
           ┌────────────┐  ┌──────────┐   ┌──────┐
           │processRes  │─▶│ classes  │──▶│ test │──▶│ jar │──▶│ build │
           └────────────┘  └──────────┘   └──────┘
           (each task: inputs/outputs tracked -> skip if UP-TO-DATE)

  ── State Diagram: a Gradle Task ───────────────────────────

  [inputs unchanged] ──────────────▶ [UP-TO-DATE] (skipped)
  [inputs changed]   ──execute──────▶ [EXECUTED]  (outputs refreshed)
  [output in cache]  ──FROM-CACHE───▶ [reused]     (downloaded, not rebuilt)

  ── Call Chain (Gradle build) ──────────────────────────────

  1. gradlew build        → connect to warm daemon
  2.   → configure project (build.gradle.kts)
  3.   → build task graph (build dependsOn jar dependsOn test ...)
  4.   → for each task: compare inputs -> run or mark UP-TO-DATE
  5.   → :compileJava CHANGED -> recompile
  6.   → :jar -> assemble build/libs/*.jar
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Maven and Gradle are both JVM build and dependency-management tools, and the differences come down to philosophy. Maven is declarative and convention-driven — you configure it with XML in a pom.xml, and it runs a fixed lifecycle of ordered phases: validate, compile, test, package, verify, install, deploy. That rigidity is its strength, because every Maven project builds the same way and any engineer can read any pom instantly. Gradle is programmable and flexible — you configure it with a Groovy or Kotlin DSL, and instead of a fixed lifecycle it builds a directed graph of tasks where each task declares its dependencies and Gradle computes the order.

The difference that usually decides it is performance. Gradle has three speed features Maven lacks out of the box. Incremental builds: Gradle tracks each task's inputs and outputs and skips any task whose inputs have not changed, marking it up-to-date. The build cache: Gradle reuses task outputs across builds and even across machines, so if a teammate already compiled the same code you download the result. And the daemon: a long-lived warm JVM in the background avoids cold-start cost on every build. On a large multi-module codebase this makes Gradle noticeably faster, while Maven tends to reprocess more eagerly.

On dependencies, both resolve transitive dependencies and both consume the same Maven Central artifacts. Maven centralizes versions through a parent POM and the dependencyManagement section and BOM imports, while Gradle uses configurations like implementation and api that give finer control over what leaks onto downstream compile classpaths, which also helps large-build performance.

At National Bank of India the choice was a trade-off between governance and speed. We built the same payment-gateway service both ways. Maven's uniformity made audits and onboarding easier because every project looked identical, which is why many regulated banks standardize on it. Gradle's incremental builds and caching cut our rebuild time dramatically on the larger modules, which teams with big codebases value highly. Both are excellent tools — the right answer depends on project size, build complexity, and whether the team prioritizes predictability or raw build speed.

---

keyPoints: Maven: convention over configuration, lifecycle phases
Gradle: flexible, Groovy/Kotlin DSL, faster incremental builds
mvn install: compile+test+package+install to local repo
Dependency management: BOM for consistent versions
